tier_reason: Benchmark code (run-benchmarks, ScriptBench/*.zef/.js/.py/.lua) and interpreter source are public, and the in-repo write-up (website/source/implementation.md) states the CPU (Intel Core Ultra 5 135U), GCC 11.4.0 for the Yolo-C++ build, with meson.build giving debugoptimized plus -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti, which is close to A. It stays at C because the fast column is a separate, undocumented checkout (pizlscript/yoloBuild) of what the author calls an incomplete, unsound port, and the QuickJS richards script runs 20x the work of the other ports, so the first-party comparison is not a clean run against the baseline.

corrections.baseline: QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 (release binary qjs-linux-x86_64), Lua 5.4.7 (built with GCC 11.4.0), CPython 3.10 (Ubuntu 22.04 package)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Write-up 'Raw Data' table, which matches run-benchmarks-results-1776652178.csv, gives geomean seconds: CPython 3.10 0.1296, Lua 5.4.7 0.0577, QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 0.2036, Zef Fil-C++ build #21 (no asserts) 0.2759, Zef in Yolo-C++ 0.0686. The author's table states Yolo-C++ Zef is 1.889x faster than CPython, 1.189x slower than Lua and 2.968x faster than QuickJS-ng; the memory-safe Fil-C++ build is 2.13x slower than CPython, 4.781x slower than Lua and 1.355x slower than QuickJS-ng. Per row, Yolo-C++ Zef beats QuickJS-ng on splay (0.3992 vs 0.7090), richards (0.0309 vs 0.7193) and deltablue (0.0784 vs 0.1585) but not nbody (0.0233 vs 0.0214); it beats CPython on all four rows and Lua only on splay and deltablue. The QuickJS-ng richards figure covers 20 runs of the benchmark (ScriptBench/richards.js loops runRichards() 20 times) while the Zef, Lua and Python ports run it once; dividing that row by 20 gives about 0.036 s per run, so Yolo-C++ Zef is about 1.16x faster on richards and about 1.40x faster than QuickJS-ng on the geomean, not 2.97x (derived from page data). The write-up's own headline is a 16x speed-up (67x with the Yolo-C++ port) that brings the interpreter 'into the ballpark' of QuickJS, CPython and Lua.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Fast column: Yolo-C++ build with GCC 11.4.0 (write-up); meson.build sets buildtype=debugoptimized (-O2 -g), cpp_std=c++20, -fno-exceptions, -fno-rtti, -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_NONE. The exact configure command and source revision of the pizlscript/yoloBuild directory are not stated. Memory-safe columns: Fil-C++ 0.677 (write-up; README asks for 0.678 or later) with the same meson.build.
corrections.workload: ScriptBench1 run by run-benchmarks: nbody (5000 advance steps), splay (32 runs on an 8000-node tree), richards (one run with COUNT 10000 in the Zef, Lua and Python ports, but 20 runs in richards.js) and deltablue (20 rounds of chainTest(100) plus projectionTest(100); the JS port adds one extra projectionTest). Wall-clock seconds of the whole process including interpreter startup, averaged over randomly interleaved runs (write-up says 30; the script defaults to --repeat 3), with a geomean row.
corrections.caveats: First-party, four benchmarks only. The QuickJS-ng richards column runs 20x the work of the other ports, inflating the QuickJS-ng comparison (about 1.40x rather than 2.97x after correction, derived from page data). The fast Yolo-C++ build is, in the author's words, an incomplete and unsound port: GC allocations become calloc and memory is never freed, which only survives because the benchmarks are short; it was built from a separate checkout (pizlscript/yoloBuild) whose revision is not stated. The memory-safe Fil-C++ build documented in the README is slower than all three baselines. Wall-clock timing includes process startup, and several rows run only 14-40 ms. Splay's Python and Lua ports were written with Claude; the Lua richards check uses 'or' instead of 'and'. No LICENSE file (LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt and COPYING return 404) and the README names no licence, hence reference only. The write-up is checked into the repo at website/source/implementation.md, so its text was read directly.

notes: Numbers match the CSV and the in-repo write-up, but the 2.97x win over QuickJS-ng is inflated because ScriptBench/richards.js runs runRichards() 20 times while the other ports run it once; corrected it is about 1.40x (derived). The fast build is an incomplete Yolo-C++ port that never frees memory (author calls it unsound), and the memory-safe Fil-C++ build is slower than CPython, Lua and QuickJS-ng. Kept at C with no licence (reference); not a reject because the CPython and Lua comparisons are like-for-like and the author documents the flaws.

tier_reason: The README numbers are first-party (Ryzen 7 7840HS, no Go version; benchmark code lives in the separate ngocphuongnb/go-js-engines-benchmark repo, whose published numbers differ), which alone is C. Raised to B because an independent run by the ModerncQuickJS maintainer (gitlab cznic/quickjs commit 6488255: compare/compare_test.go via 'go test -vet=off -run @ -bench . -benchtime 5s', AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Go 1.23.0 per the diff, QJS v0.0.3) also measures QJS faster than goja and slightly faster than ModerncQuickJS; it might reach A if the Go toolchain line is confirmed as the compiler actually used rather than the go.mod directive.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (first-party, AMD Ryzen 7 7840HS): factorial(10) x 1,000,000 averages 746.132 ms vs goja 1.127 s (1.51x) and ModerncQuickJS 1.910 s (2.56x); V8 v7 score 498 vs goja 442 and ModerncQuickJS 323, suite duration 72.004 s vs 78.349 s and 97.240 s. QJS loses the RegExp row to both goja (381) and ModerncQuickJS (145) with 142. Independent run (cznic/quickjs commit 6488255, Oct 8 2025, AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Go 1.23.0, QJS v0.0.3): geomean ns/op relative to ModerncQuickJS (CCGO) 1.000, QJS 0.950, goja 1.636, i.e. QJS about 1.72x faster than goja and about 1.05x faster than ModerncQuickJS (derived from page data); QJS is 13.895x slower than CCGO on map_set_bigint.js and 0.424 on func_call.js. A competing project's run (go-quickjs/go-js-engines-benchmark, Apple M5 Max, Go 1.27.0, Oct 5 2026) has factorial averages QJS 592.033 ms vs goja 703.527 ms and ModerncQuickJS 653.106 ms, and V8 v7 scores QJS 761 vs goja 751 vs ModerncQuickJS 787.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README run: Go version and build flags not stated. Independent cznic run: Go 1.23.0 (per the commit diff), go test -vet=off -timeout 24h -run @ -bench . -benchtime 5s piped through compare/benchreport.go.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7840HS, 32GB RAM, Linux (README); independent cznic run on AMD Ryzen 9 3900X 12-Core, linux/amd64
corrections.workload: README: factorial(10) computed 1,000,000 times (five iterations) and the AreWeFastYet V8 version 7 suite. Independent cznic run: the modernc.org/quickjs compare suite of JavaScript microbenchmarks (array_for, array_for_in, func_call, global_read, map_set_bigint, string_build_large1 and others) run as Go benchmarks.
corrections.caveats: QJS is quickjs-ng (git submodule qjswasm/quickjs points at quickjs-ng/quickjs) compiled to WebAssembly and run on wazero with Go bindings, so it is a wrapper of an already-listed engine; its claim is only against other Go-embedded engines (goja, ModerncQuickJS) and it is not compared against native C QuickJS. README numbers are first-party with no Go version or build flags; the author's benchmark repo (ngocphuongnb/go-js-engines-benchmark, same CPU) publishes different figures (factorial 717.258 ms; V8 score 522 vs goja 452 vs ModerncQuickJS 343). An independent run by the ModerncQuickJS maintainer on QJS v0.0.3 shows a smaller lead (about 1.72x over goja and 1.05x over ModerncQuickJS on geomean, derived) and a 13.9x loss on map_set_bigint. A competing project's run on Apple M5 Max puts ModerncQuickJS ahead of QJS on the V8 v7 score (787 vs 761) with goja close behind (751). QJS loses the RegExp test in its own README table. Last commit 2025-10-28, so it turns stale after 2026-10-28.

notes: README numbers match exactly; tier raised C to B on an independent cznic/quickjs run (Ryzen 9 3900X) that also shows QJS ahead of goja, though by less (about 1.72x geomean, derived) and only about 5% ahead of ModerncQuickJS. It is quickjs-ng compiled to Wasm on wazero with Go bindings, a wrapper of the listed https://github.com/quickjs-ng/quickjs, so the orchestrator may want decision duplicate under the wrapper rule. Shortcomings: first-party README without Go version, loses RegExp, a competitor's M5 Max run has ModerncQuickJS ahead (787 vs 761), and a 13.9x loss on map_set_bigint in the independent run.
